ch07.card: Part 6 of 10. Writing down the answer.
ch07.s01.c1: The last part inside the model is the talker.
ch07.s01.c2: Its job is one line at the end of each turn of thinking. It adds no thinking.
ch07.s01.c3: New design, untested. Thoughts in, calls and answer out. No pointer.
ch07.s01.c4: Today's talker is a small stand-in. It also copies where the thinker points. The answer, 10, is made up.
ch07.s02.c1: Picture a toolbox. Today's talker is a small stand-in with three ways to write.
ch07.s02.c2: Copy and paste: span copy takes a stretch of letters from the question or the notes.
ch07.s02.c3: Point at a word: a word pointer, a learned pick of a spot, takes one whole word from the question.
ch07.s02.c4: Spell it out: letter slots spell the answer when it is not in the text. Made-up examples. The planned talker has no pointer.
ch07.s03.c1: In today's stand-in, a pointer lands on the last digit of the last reply: the 0.
ch07.s03.c2: The copy steps one letter left and takes the 1.
ch07.s03.c3: Next to the left is a space. A small learned part, the stop head, says stop.
ch07.s03.c4: The digits came out last first, 0 then 1. Plain code flips them to read 10. The plan has no pointer.
ch07.s04.c1: In the tested version, in all 6 copies of the 3-million-number model with an outside calculator, called T1SDR, the stand-in's span copy wrote 91.5% of answers.
ch07.s04.c2: That counts how often it was used on 400 familiar calculator questions, not how often it was right.
ch07.s04.c3: The stand-in's pointer and stop head are learned. Three small pieces are hand-written code.
ch07.s04.c4: The plan: one learned writer replaces them, for calls and answers. Not run.
ch07.s05.c1: What if the answer is not in the text? Then today's stand-in spells it, in letter slots.
ch07.s05.c2: Today there are 9 places: room for 8 letters and an end mark. Each place picks a letter, or copies one.
ch07.s05.c3: They fill last letter first, so yes comes out as s, e, y. The code flips it. Yes is a made-up answer.
ch07.s06.c1: What if the answer is longer than the room? Today's slots hold 8 letters. A longer training answer would be cut.
ch07.s06.c2: That never happened. Of 200,000 training answers, 0 were longer than 8.
ch07.s06.c3: But hiding a word of 9 to 12 letters, in fill-in-the-blank practice, would hit it.
ch07.s06.c4: The finished design, B3, writes up to 35 letters and counts longer answers.
ch07.s06.c5: A count above 0 fails its pass mark, set in advance. Blanks of 9 to 12 letters are safe only here. Built, but never run.
ch07.s07.c1: Now the empty seat. The plan has a talker of about 25 million numbers. It writes English, no pointer.
ch07.s07.c2: Not built. As built, the 100M-thinker design is 373.1M in all: 271.0M borrowed, frozen reader, Gemma, plus 102.1M trained.
ch07.s07.c3: How it would learn English is not in the plan. A separate team session owns that. Today: short answers only. No sentences.
ch07.s08.c1: An older, different design now, built on borrowed language models. Not today's talker. Borrowed means somebody else trained them.
ch07.s08.c2: With a 350-million-number language model as reader and talker, our system scored 66.1. With 1.2 billion: 92.6.
ch07.s08.c3: A small copy talker scored 13.6 on question kinds it never practised. The language-model talker scored 78.2. English from scratch is not shown.
ch07.s09.c1: What if we switch the thinking off? One check did, on one trained copy at 3M. This is the older design, with 12 rounds.
ch07.s09.c2: Thinking on scored 73.01. Thinking off scored 0.66, on 6,040 questions kept aside.
ch07.s09.c3: That hints the talker cannot answer alone. One copy is only a hint. Hold that thought.
ch07.s09.c4: Twist: an earlier Gemma-reader copy scored 18.09 on familiar questions with zero rounds, so cannot is not shown.
ch07.s10.c1: Where could it learn English? FineWeb-Edu, free web text, enters practice as fill-in-the-blank rows.
ch07.s10.c2: One word of 3 to 12 letters is hidden, and the model must name it.
ch07.s10.c3: So this kind of practice teaches reading English, not writing it.
ch07.s10.c4: By plan, 84% of the practice text in the planned big training run is web text. Plan only.
ch07.s11.c1: The plan's final proof is a race against small public models, such as SmolLM2-360M.
ch07.s11.c2: To win, it must be ahead by at least 3 points on our own kept-aside tests, and ahead on a question set called bAbI.
ch07.s11.c3: The whole size is counted, borrowed numbers too. The race needs the English talker, which does not exist yet. Neither is expected by the Oct 31 results readout.
ch07.s12.c1: The plan: thoughts in, calls and answer out, no pointer.
ch07.s12.c2: Today's stand-in copies by pointer. Tested only at 3M.
ch07.s12.c3: The English talker is a placeholder, a spot saved for something not built. Next: how the parts we train learn by practice, one small nudge at a time.
